title: The surah before sleep
hookLine: the Prophet ﷺ recited al-Mulk before sleeping, and it intercedes for its reader (Tirmidhi)

cards: What's the last thing you see before you sleep? For a lot of people it's a phone: one more video, one more scroll, blue light on the ceiling. In many Muslim homes there's an older habit for the last minutes of the day.
A short chapter, thirty verses, about five or ten minutes read aloud. Children learn it early. Grandparents say it from memory in the dark.
It's surah sixty-seven, al-Mulk, the Sovereignty.

teach.b: It begins, in Pickthall: "Blessed is He in Whose hand is the Sovereignty, and, He is Able to do all things." Al-mulk: the dominion, the kingship over everything.
The first word, tabaraka, blessed, is why many people simply call the surah Tabarak. Two hadith in at-Tirmidhi's collection explain the bedtime habit.

teach.h: THE PROPHET READ IT BEFORE SLEEP.
teach.b: In one, a companion reports that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ would not sleep until he had recited two surahs: as-Sajdah, and Tabarak, al-Mulk.
In the other, the Prophet says a surah of the Qur'an, thirty verses long, interceded for a man until he was forgiven, and he names it: Tabarak alladhi biyadihi al-mulk.
To intercede is to speak up for someone, the way a friend might stand beside you in a hard meeting and say, I know this person. In the hadith, a surah does the speaking.

Other narrations call al-Mulk a protector, and many Muslims understand it as a shield for its reader in the grave. Scholars discuss how strong each narration is; the habit of reading it at night is very widely kept.
And look at what the surah holds, because we'll spend three more days inside it. Death and life. The sky, looked at again and again.
The earth made easy to walk on. Birds held up in the air.
It's a surah about being held. Maybe that's why it suits the moment a person lets go of the day and can't hold anything themselves.

how: Many Muslims recite surah al-Mulk (also called Tabarak) every night before sleeping, following hadith that the Prophet did so and that this thirty-verse surah intercedes for its reader; children often learn it by heart.

games.q: it's night. by the hadith in Tirmidhi, which two surahs did the Prophet recite before he slept?
games.why: as-Sajdah and Tabarak, al-Mulk. many Muslims keep the same habit at bedtime.

practice: Say the first verse, or hear it in your head: blessed is He in whose hand is the sovereignty. Notice your own hands and what they've been holding today, and let them rest open on your knees.
Many keep all thirty verses for the last minutes before sleep, in Arabic or in any translation.

wordCard.voice: Al-Mulk. The Sovereignty, surah sixty-seven, thirty verses the Prophet read before sleeping, which a hadith says interceded for its reader. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: blessed is He, the first word of al-Mulk, and the surah's popular name.

carryVoice: Your line: it intercedes. A surah that speaks up for its reader. Rest well tonight.
